name: José Joaquín de Olmedo International Airport
before:
Ecuador's second busiest airport, on the Avenida de las Americas and only 5 km north of central Guayaquil, which makes for an unusually short airport transfer.

The airport sits in the flat delta of the Guayas River with level ground on every side, and the 2,790 metre runway takes aircraft as large as a 747 or an A340-600. A domestic expansion in 2014 lifted capacity to around 7.5 million passengers a year.

One thing to flag when quoting: an exit tax is charged on all international tickets out of this airport. Check whether the fare a client is looking at already includes it.

The airport is named after Jose Joaquin de Olmedo, a poet who was the first mayor of Guayaquil and later president of Ecuador. It was previously called Simon Bolivar International, a name still used by airports in Venezuela and Colombia, so be careful which one a supplier means.
after:
Ecuador's second busiest airport, on the Avenida de las Américas and 5 km north of central Guayaquil.

The single runway is 2,790 metres long. An enlarged domestic terminal opened in July 2014, lifting capacity to more than 7 million passengers a year.

One thing to know when quoting: the international departure tax is included in the ticket price, so it is not paid at the airport.

The airport is named after José Joaquín de Olmedo. It was previously called Simón Bolívar International, a name still used by airports in Venezuela and Colombia, so be careful which one a supplier means.

claims.note: Guayaquil's own municipal airport authority says so on its live site. INEC's latest airport-level split (bulletin of August 2025, 2024 figures from the DGAC) has Guayaquil second to Quito for international passengers, about 1.06 million arrivals and 1.16 million departures in thousands against Quito's 1.27 and 1.24 million, far ahead of Manta; the DGAC's 2025 figures put it second for cargo too. No 2025 passenger total for Guayaquil could be read: its operator publishes none on its site, and the DGAC's 2025 bulletin sits behind its intranet login.

claims.wasBefore: which makes for an unusually short airport transfer
claims.why: 'Unusually' is a comparison no source makes. The distance itself is kept. The clause is not softened to 'a short transfer' either: the FCDO advises against all but essential travel to Guayas province, Guayaquil included, with only airside transit at the airport exempt (held back below), so the text should not sell the trip into town.

claims.claim: FCDO: against all but essential travel to Guayas province; state of emergency and curfew
claims.why: Held back, and recommended for Andy: the FCDO (updated 16 September 2026) advises against all but essential travel to Guayas and six other coastal provinces, with airside transit within Guayaquil Airport exempt. A 60-day state of emergency from 15 September covers Guayas, with a curfew from midnight to 5am in Guayas and three other provinces from 17 to 30 September. The FCDO also says Guayaquil's murder rate is very high, and that there are authorised taxi booths at Quito and Guayaquil international airports. Nothing in the old text to replace, so under the like-for-like rule it stays out, but it is the single most important thing a UK agent should know about this airport.

Useful to an agent, but nothing in the old text to replace.

claims.claim: who flies here and who runs it
claims.why: Held back: the operator lists Avianca and Latam for domestic routes and Air Europa, American Airlines, Avianca, Copa Airlines, KLM, Latam, Iberia and JetBlue for international ones; its board on 23 September 2026 shows KLM to Amsterdam and Iberia to Madrid. TAGSA, part of Corporación América Airports, runs the airport under a concession from the city's airport authority until 27 July 2031. The old text names no airline or operator.
